claims.text: Adding approximately 2–5 atomic percent of an element with strong phosphorus affinity will improve the glass-forming ability of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
The minor additive will increase the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
An early transition metal having a strongly negative mixing enthalpy with phosphorus is a candidate additive.
The intervention will be effective at cooling rates that are marginal for glass formation.
The additive's influence may be reduced at extremely high cooling rates.
The additive's influence may be reduced when its chemical interaction with phosphorus is weak.
Preferential interactions between the additive and phosphorus will enhance chemical short-range order.
Preferential interactions between the additive and phosphorus will increase atomic-scale disorder.
The additive-induced local chemical environment will impede atomic diffusion.
The additive-induced local chemical environment will impede the atomic rearrangements required for crystalline nucleation during cooling and heating.
The local disorder will raise the critical cooling rate needed to bypass crystallization.
The local disorder will increase the crystallization onset temperature during heating.
Relative to the additive-free baseline, the modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate.
Relative to the additive-free baseline, the modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature.
An excessively high additive concentration may eliminate or reverse the favorable effects.
An additive lacking sufficiently strong phosphorus affinity may fail to produce the favorable effects.
An excessively high or chemically unsuitable additive concentration may promote phase separation.
An excessively high or chemically unsuitable additive concentration may promote alternative crystallization pathways.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says the intervention raises the critical cooling rate, whereas the predicted outcome says it lowers the critical cooling rate. Lowering, not raising, the critical cooling rate conventionally corresponds to improved glass-forming ability.
